# CIVA Glider downgrades

These descriptions are generated from the Tuning package of FCScore and describe what FCScore measures for each downgrade. See the [downgrade reference](index.md) for how to read them.

Generated from Tuning commit: `e3d5e7b`.

**Rulebook source**

> - [FAI Sporting Code Section 6, Part 2, Glider Aircraft, Version 2026 V3](https://www.civanews.com/wp-content/uploads/Section6_Part2_v2026-V3.pdf) (CIVA-G)
>
> This configuration is for glider aerobatics under the CIVA rules. It starts from the IAC glider configuration and changes the measurements, settings and references that the CIVA glider rules treat differently.
>
> The judging references in `judging_guide.json` are verbatim extracts from CIVA-G, identified by their paragraph number: the downgrades applicable to figures (4.5), the penalties (4.4), the performance zone and height limits (3.4, 3.9) and Appendix B, the criteria for judging glider aerobatic figures. The box limits are contest penalties in the rules rather than figure deductions, so the FCScore box downgrades are estimates of their severity.
>
> What the configuration models:
>
> - **Glide path.** Horizontal lines, turns and rolling turns may be flown with a flight path from level to 10° below the horizon (B.8.1.2, B.9.2.5 d, B.9.3.6 b), and the entry and exit lines of a loop may differ within that bracket (B.9.10.2). FCScore charges one point per 5° outside the bracket where a figure starts or ends on a horizontal line, and charges any change in the angle during a line or turn.
> - **Competition turns** must be exactly 60° of bank (B.9.2.5 a), charged one point per 5° on either side.
> - **Flick rolls** need not be centred on an interior line (B.8.1.8). A line is left out of the line length comparison only when every roll on it is a flick roll, and aileron and hesitation rolls must still be centred. Flick rolls on a loop must still be centred (B.9.10.4).
> - **Tailslides** need only slide backwards a visible amount (B.9.6.1). A missing slide costs about 4 points.
> - **Spins and flick rolls** that never stall, or never autorotate, are 4 point deductions in CIVA-G (B.9.27.6, B.9.25.2), so the spin and snap fault lookups reach about 4 points instead of 10.
> - **Categories** are Unlimited and Advanced (1.2.2.1). Both fly in a 1000 x 1000 m performance zone between 200 m and 1200 m over datum (3.4.1.1, 3.9.1.1).
>
> What it does not model:
>
> - A flick roll whose autorotation ends with more than 45° of rotation remaining is awarded 0.0 (B.9.25.5). FCScore charges early stops on a graded scale without the step to zero.
> - The 50 m tolerance around the performance zone (4.4.2.1) and the 750 m upper limit of a split programme (3.9.1.1 b).
> - Positioning marks, interruptions and the other contest penalties.
>
> The Positioning references (4.1.5, 2.3.4, B.10) are the sequence-level positioning mark: the judges' mark (25K Unlimited, 20K Advanced) plus the electronic tracking mark (15K). FCScore gives one score with the combined K factor (40K, 35K), from the box deductions of all the figures.

Rulebook extracts are quoted verbatim and listed under [Rulebook references](#rulebook-references).

## Intra-element downgrades

### Horizontal Line Climb {#climb}

`climb`

Checks that horizontal lines are flown on a constant glide path. A flight path from level to 10° below the horizon is allowed, and any change in the angle during the line is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Horizontal lines are judged on the flight path rather than the attitude. Gliders cannot hold altitude without losing speed, so the flight path of a horizontal line may be inclined between 0 and 10° below the horizon, and deviations above or below this bracket cost one point for every 5° (CIVA-G B.8.1.2, 4.5.1.3). Within the bracket the pilot may choose the angle, but any change in it during the line is charged.

    FCScore measures how the angle between the aircraft's flight path and the horizontal changes over each horizontal line, relative to the angle at the start of the line, taken as no lower than level and no higher than 10° below the horizon. It charges each increase in the difference; a decrease is free. A constant glide from level to 10° below the horizon therefore costs nothing, and any change in the angle is charged. A line that starts outside the bracket, climbing or more than 10° below the horizon, is measured from the nearest edge of the bracket; the angle outside the bracket is charged on the element that creates it, so it is not charged again here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule. The line between two figures belongs to the next figure, so what is measured on the exit line of a figure is reported with the following figure, and the figure's own score keeps the rest.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> All lines are judged in relation to the true horizon and the Aerobatic Box axes. Horizontal lines are judged on flight path, not attitude.
>
> [B.8.1.1](#rb-lines.horizontal)

> Horizontal lines in glider aerobatics may be inclined between zero (0) and ten (10) degrees below the horizon. … Deviations above or below this bracket will be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.
>
> [4.5.1.3, B.8.1.2](#rb-gliders.glide_bracket)

> For deviations from the correct geometry (plane of flight, direction of flight, angle of bank) and for deviations from the proper flight path or the proper attitude (as appropriate), the mark will be reduced by 1 point per 5 degrees of deviation.
>
> [4.5.1.1](#rb-general.angle_rule)

### Horizontal Line Heading {#heading}

`heading`

Checks that the nose stays parallel to the box axis on horizontal lines. Only growth in the heading error is charged, so swinging back is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    On horizontal lines the aircraft's heading must remain parallel to the X or Y axis of the box. A pilot may correct for wind drift, but if the correction is visible to the judge the standard deduction of one point per 5° of heading deviation applies.

    FCScore measures the angle of the fuselage, not the flight path, relative to the template heading in the horizontal plane, and charges each increase in the absolute angle over the line; a decrease is free. Because the nose direction is measured, a visible crab against a crosswind shows up here, but only the part that builds up during the line is charged. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule. The line between two figures belongs to the next figure, so what is measured on the exit line of a figure is reported with the following figure, and the figure's own score keeps the rest.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> While maintaining a horizontal flight path, the aircraft's longitudinal axis must remain parallel to the X or Y axis. The deduction for deviation in either axis is one (1) point per five (5) degrees from the correct geometry.
>
> [B.8.1.3](#rb-lines.heading)

> A common flight mode is to crab into the wind as done in navigational flight. … The downside to this approach is that if the aircraft longitudinal axis is detected by the Judge to be at an angle to the competition axis (main or secondary), one (1) point per five (5) degrees must be deducted.
>
> [B.7.1.5](#rb-general.wind_correction)

### Vertical/45° Line Yaw {#yaw}

`yaw`

Checks that the nose does not swing sideways on vertical and 45° lines. Only growth in the sideways attitude error is charged, so swinging back is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Vertical and 45° lines are judged on the attitude of the aircraft, according to its zero-lift axis, not on the flight path, so wind drift is ignored but the aircraft must point exactly along the line. The wings must also stay aligned with a box axis and the horizon.

    FCScore measures the angle of the fuselage relative to the template line in the sideways (yaw) direction and charges each increase in the absolute angle over the line; a decrease is free. It uses the fuselage centre-line as the reference rather than your zero-lift axis, which it does not know. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Judging vertical lines is based on the attitude of the aircraft and not its flight path. When an aircraft's flight path, in a zero-wind condition, is exactly 90 degrees to the horizon, the wings are being held at the correct angle to produce no lift. The aircraft's attitude while in this condition (zero lift) defines the proper judging criterion for vertical attitude. This is called the zero-lift axis.
>
> [B.3.2.1](#rb-lines.vertical)

> This is the vertical attitude plus or minus 45 degrees. … These changes in the flight path angle must also be ignored when judging 45 degree lines. The prescribed deduction is one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation from the correct geometry (0.5 points per 2.5 degrees).
>
> [B.3.3.1, B.3.3.2](#rb-lines.diagonal)

### Turn Altitude Change {#axial_track}

`axial_track`

Checks that turns and rolling turns are flown on a constant glide path. A flight path from level to 10° below the horizon is allowed, and any change in the angle around the turn is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    In turns and rolling turns the aircraft must maintain a constant glide, 0 to 10° below the horizon, throughout the figure, and any deviation above or below that bracket costs one point for every 5° (B.9.2.5 d, B.9.3.6 b). The turn is not wind corrected, but the pilot must still hold the glide.

    FCScore measures how the angle between the flight path and the horizontal plane of the turn changes around the turn, relative to the angle at the start of the turn, taken as no lower than level and no higher than 10° below the horizon. It charges each increase in the difference; a decrease is free. It applies to horizontal arcs such as turns and rolling turns, and not to loops in a vertical plane. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The aircraft must maintain a constant glide (0 to 10 degrees below the horizon) throughout the figure. Any deviation above or below is one (1) point for every five (5) degrees. … Variations from the constant glide (0 to 10 degrees below the horizon) are deducted by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.
>
> [B.9.2.5 d, B.9.3.6 b](#rb-turns.altitude)

> Horizontal lines in glider aerobatics may be inclined between zero (0) and ten (10) degrees below the horizon. … Deviations above or below this bracket will be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.
>
> [4.5.1.3, B.8.1.2](#rb-gliders.glide_bracket)

### Loop Plane Attitude {#axial_attitude}

`axial_attitude`

Checks that the nose stays in the plane of the loop. Only growth in the out-of-plane angle of the fuselage is charged, so swinging back is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A looping line is a vertically curving path that must have a constant radius. Loops must be flown with no visible crabbing, at one point for every 5° (B.9.10.3).

    FCScore measures the angle of the fuselage out of the plane of the loop and charges each increase in the absolute angle; a decrease is free. It measures the direction the nose points, so a crab angle held against a crosswind shows up here, even though the rules give no deduction for the loop's finish being displaced sideways by crosswind. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Loops must be flown with no visible crabbing and wings must be level at all times. The one (1) point for every five (5) degrees rule holds for both these cases.
>
> [B.9.10.3](#rb-loops.crab_wings)

> For deviations from the correct geometry (plane of flight, direction of flight, angle of bank) and for deviations from the proper flight path or the proper attitude (as appropriate), the mark will be reduced by 1 point per 5 degrees of deviation.
>
> [4.5.1.1](#rb-general.angle_rule)

### Loop Exit Flight Path {#radial_track}

`radial_track`

Checks the flight path when a loop returns to horizontal flight. A flight path from level to 10° below the horizon is free; the angle outside that bracket at the end of the loop is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    When a looping line returns to a horizontal line, that line is judged on flight path. The entry and exit lines of a glider loop may be inclined between 0 and 10° below the horizon, and the inclination may differ between them within that bracket (B.9.10.2); deviations above or below the bracket cost one point for every 5° (B.8.1.2).

    FCScore takes the last point of the loop and charges the angle by which the flight path in the plane of the loop is outside the bracket from level to 10° below the horizon; an angle inside the bracket is free. It is an absolute measure at the end of the loop, so an over- or under-flown arc beyond the bracket is charged here once and the line that follows is only charged for further change. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> All lines are judged in relation to the true horizon and the Aerobatic Box axes. Horizontal lines are judged on flight path, not attitude.
>
> [B.8.1.1](#rb-lines.horizontal)

> Horizontal lines in glider aerobatics may be inclined between zero (0) and ten (10) degrees below the horizon. … Deviations above or below this bracket will be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.
>
> [4.5.1.3, B.8.1.2](#rb-gliders.glide_bracket)

> In glider aerobatics, the entry and exit lines of the loop may be inclined 0 to 10 degrees below the horizon and the inclination may be different for entry and exit lines within the above tolerances
>
> [B.9.10.2](#rb-gliders.loop_lines)

### Loop Exit Attitude {#radial_attitude}

`radial_attitude`

Checks that the aircraft points exactly along the following line when a loop ends on a vertical or 45° line. The full attitude error at the end of the loop is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Vertical and 45° lines are judged on attitude, so when a loop ends on one the aircraft must be pointing exactly along that line as the loop finishes, within one point per 5° of error.

    FCScore takes the last point of the loop and charges the whole angle between the fuselage and the template within the plane of the loop. It is an absolute measure at the end of the loop, so an over- or under-flown arc is charged here once and the line that follows is only charged for further change. It also applies at the end of horizontal arcs. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Judging vertical lines is based on the attitude of the aircraft and not its flight path. When an aircraft's flight path, in a zero-wind condition, is exactly 90 degrees to the horizon, the wings are being held at the correct angle to produce no lift. The aircraft's attitude while in this condition (zero lift) defines the proper judging criterion for vertical attitude. This is called the zero-lift axis.
>
> [B.3.2.1](#rb-lines.vertical)

> This is the vertical attitude plus or minus 45 degrees. … These changes in the flight path angle must also be ignored when judging 45 degree lines. The prescribed deduction is one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation from the correct geometry (0.5 points per 2.5 degrees).

### Roll Angle on Lines {#line_roll}

`line_roll`

Checks that the wings stay aligned on lines without a roll, and that there is no rolling during a stall turn or tailslide. Only growth in the roll angle error is charged, so levelling the wings again is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    On vertical lines the wings must be aligned with a box axis and the horizon, and during a stall turn pivot there must be no rolling or pitching motion, at one point per 5°. A tailslide is judged in the same way.

    FCScore measures the roll angle relative to the template on lines that contain no roll, and through stall turns and tailslides, and charges each increase in the absolute roll error; a decrease is free. An angle already present at the start of the element is not charged again, as it was charged where it arose. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule. The line between two figures belongs to the next figure, so what is measured on the exit line of a figure is reported with the following figure, and the figure's own score keeps the rest.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> During the vertical climb or vertical descent, the wings must remain parallel to the horizon. There will be a one (1) point deduction per five (5) degrees, when the line connecting both wing tips deviates from horizontal.
>
> [B.9.5.2 e](#rb-lines.vertical_wings)

> There must be no rotation around the longitudinal or lateral axes. If there is movement around any axis other than the yaw axis, often referred to as "torquing" … there is a deduction of one (1) point for each five (5) degrees off axis.
>
> [B.9.5.2 h](#rb-stall_turns.pivot_motion)
