### Roll Angle in Rolling Turn Pauses {#circle_pause_roll}

`circle_pause_roll`

Checks that the wings stay at the template attitude during a brief pause between the rolls of a rolling turn. Only growth in the roll angle error is charged, so returning to the attitude is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A rolling turn may pause briefly where the roll direction changes. At a roll direction reversal the wings must be level, and errors in the roll angle from wings level cost one point for every 5° (B.9.3.6 e). FCScore applies the same rule to the pause.

    FCScore measures the roll angle relative to the template on the short level loop segments that sit between two rolling segments of a turn, and charges each increase in the absolute roll error; a decrease is free. An angle already present at the start of the pause is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At a roll direction reversal there must be only a short pause, with the wings level. A longer pause is no more than a one (1) point deduction. Errors in the roll angle from wings level are deducted using one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [B.9.3.6 e](#rb-turns.rolling_reversal)

> For deviations from the correct geometry (plane of flight, direction of flight, angle of bank) and for deviations from the proper flight path or the proper attitude (as appropriate), the mark will be reduced by 1 point per 5 degrees of deviation.
>
> [4.5.1.1](#rb-general.angle_rule)

### Bank Angle in Turns {#turn_roll}

`turn_roll`

Checks that the bank angle established for a turn is held. Only growth in the bank angle error during the turn is charged, so returning to the bank is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    The angle of bank established by the roll that starts a competition turn must be exactly 60°, and once established it must remain constant: any deviation costs one point for every 5° (B.9.2.5 a, b).

    FCScore measures how the bank angle differs from the angle established at the start of the turn, taking an established bank below or above 60° as 60°, and charges each increase in the absolute error; a decrease is free. How far the established bank is from 60° is charged by Turn Entry Bank Angle. It applies to turns that contain no roll. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The turn must maintain 60 degrees of bank throughout. … The angle of bank, once established, must remain constant. Any deviation is a one (1) point deduction for every five (5) degrees of deviation.
>
> [B.9.2.3, B.9.2.5 b](#rb-turns.bank)

> This must be a roll of 60 degrees, it must be performed on the entry heading, and the aircraft must maintain a constant glide (0 to 10 degrees below the horizon). … The angle of bank established by the initial rolling manoeuvre must be exactly 60 degrees. Any deviation is a one (1) point deduction for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [B.9.2.2, B.9.2.5 a](#rb-turns.entry_bank)

### Roll Rotation Amount {#roll_roll}

`roll_roll`

Checks that a roll, snap or spin finishes at the planned attitude. At the point of maximum rotation, the roll attitude is compared with the planned attitude and the difference is charged once, so both over- and under-rotation count. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A roll must end with a precise stop, with the wings at the desired degree of rotation, and over- or under-rotation costs one point for every 5°. A snap or spin must also end at its prescribed rotation.

    FCScore finds the point of maximum rotation in each roll, snap or spin and compares the aircraft's roll attitude there with the planned attitude. It assesses the final attitude, not the total number of degrees rolled, although it tracks the rotation continuously (allowing for the angle wrapping round at 180°) so that a roll that overshoots by a full turn is not mistaken for a correct one. Over-rotation and under-rotation are charged equally, as a single absolute error at that point. Rolling back afterwards is charged separately, and the over-rotation is not charged a second time when the pilot corrects it. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The wings must stop precisely after the desired degree of rotation and not go past the stop point and then return. This is referred to as "bumping the point". A deduction of 0.5 point to one (1) point is awarded depending on the severity of the "bump"
>
> [B.9.23.2](#rb-rolls.stop)

> Over-rotating a roll and rolling the wings back again must be penalised by 1 point per 5 degrees of over-rotation, even if the correct geometry is resumed afterwards, no matter how quickly the correction is made.
>
> [4.5.1.7](#rb-general.corrections)

### Turn Entry Bank Angle {#preturn_roll}

`preturn_roll`

Checks that the roll into a turn establishes exactly 60° of bank. Any difference from 60° at the end of the roll is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A competition turn starts by establishing a bank of exactly 60° while maintaining the entry heading, before the heading change begins. Any deviation costs one point for every 5° (B.9.2.2, B.9.2.5 a).

    FCScore takes the point of maximum rotation of the roll that precedes a turn, measures the bank angle from wings level, and charges the difference from 60°, whether the bank is shallower or steeper. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> This must be a roll of 60 degrees, it must be performed on the entry heading, and the aircraft must maintain a constant glide (0 to 10 degrees below the horizon). … The angle of bank established by the initial rolling manoeuvre must be exactly 60 degrees. Any deviation is a one (1) point deduction for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [B.9.2.2, B.9.2.5 a](#rb-turns.entry_bank)

### Roll Rebound {#rebound}

`rebound`

Checks that a roll stays where it stopped. After the maximum rotation, any growth in the roll error, such as bouncing back past the target or wobbling, is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    The rotation must end with a precise stop at the desired angle. The rules charge an over-rotation once and do not charge again for rolling the wings back to the correct geometry.

    FCScore looks at each rotating element after the point of maximum rotation and charges each increase in the absolute roll error. An over-rotation is charged once, at the point of maximum rotation, so rolling back from it is not charged again, but rolling back past the target or rocking the wings creates a new increase that is charged. A decrease in the error is free. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Over-rotating a roll and rolling the wings back again must be penalised by 1 point per 5 degrees of over-rotation, even if the correct geometry is resumed afterwards, no matter how quickly the correction is made.
>
> [4.5.1.7](#rb-general.corrections)

> The wings must stop precisely after the desired degree of rotation and not go past the stop point and then return. This is referred to as "bumping the point". A deduction of 0.5 point to one (1) point is awarded depending on the severity of the "bump"
>
> [B.9.23.2](#rb-rolls.stop)

### Roll Centring on the Loop {#loop_roll_centre}

`loop_roll_centre`

Checks that a roll, or roll combination, on a loop is centred on the apex or nadir. The angle between the middle of the rolling section and the apex is charged once for the whole section. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, and loops high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Rolls may appear on looping lines. The rolls must be centered symmetrically about the apex or nadir and be integrated into the radius. The pilot chooses how much of the loop the roll or roll combination uses, but it must take the same amount of loop before the apex as after it. A roll that is not centred is downgraded one point for every 5° of the arc that it is off centre, and a roll flown on a line at the apex costs at least two points (B.9.10.4).

    FCScore takes the whole rolling section of one loop as a single window: the rolls and snaps and the pauses between them, but not the loop flown either side of it. It reads the flight path elevation where the section starts and where it ends. The path falls through the top of a loop and rises through the bottom, so the average of the two elevations is zero when the section is centred about the apex or nadir, whatever the size and shape of the loop (round, P, Q or reversing) and however much of it the pilot uses. An error of 10° in where the roll sits on the loop is a 10° error in that average. FCScore charges its size once, at the end of the section, as an angle, so a roll centred early and one centred late cost the same. It is measured from the flown path, so a roll that misses the apex altogether is still charged for how far from it it was. Rolls and snaps on straight lines are not covered, and neither are loops whose roll fills the whole loop element, which have no apex to centre on. The extra deduction for flying part of a roll on a straight line is not measured here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Where a roll sits on a loop is easiest to judge when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where the position along the loop is hidden. It is also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side. The weighting does not depend on how much of the loop the roll uses. Large errors are counted in full.

> If there is a roll or rolls at the apex of the loop, it must be centred in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself. Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centred, it must be downgraded one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of the arc that it is off centre.
>
> [B.9.10.4](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Snap Centring on the Loop {#loop_snap_centre}

`loop_snap_centre`

Checks that a snap roll on a loop is centred on the apex or nadir. The angle between the middle of the rolling section and the apex is charged once for the whole section. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, and loops high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Unlike a flick roll on a straight line, a flick roll at the apex of a loop must still be centred (B.9.10.4). A snap roll on a loop is part of the same rolling section as the rolls on that loop, and the whole section must be centred about the apex or nadir. The snap is not scored separately: FCScore scores the rolls, snaps and pauses of the loop together as one window, under the roll centring downgrade (loop_roll_centre), and this key is only used to join the snap into it. A loop whose only roll is a snap is scored in the same way, with the snap centred on the apex.

    FCScore takes the whole rolling section of one loop as a single window: the rolls and snaps and the pauses between them, but not the loop flown either side of it. It reads the flight path elevation where the section starts and where it ends. The path falls through the top of a loop and rises through the bottom, so the average of the two elevations is zero when the section is centred about the apex or nadir, whatever the size and shape of the loop (round, P, Q or reversing) and however much of it the pilot uses. An error of 10° in where the roll sits on the loop is a 10° error in that average. FCScore charges its size once, at the end of the section, as an angle, so a roll centred early and one centred late cost the same. It is measured from the flown path, so a roll that misses the apex altogether is still charged for how far from it it was. Rolls and snaps on straight lines are not covered, and neither are loops whose roll fills the whole loop element, which have no apex to centre on. The extra deduction for flying part of a roll on a straight line is not measured here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Where a roll sits on a loop is easiest to judge when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where the position along the loop is hidden. It is also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side. The weighting does not depend on how much of the loop the roll uses. Large errors are counted in full.

> If there is a roll or rolls at the apex of the loop, it must be centred in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself. Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centred, it must be downgraded one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of the arc that it is off centre.
>
> [B.9.10.4](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Pause Centring on the Loop {#loop_pause_centre}

`loop_pause_centre`

Checks that a pause between rolls on a loop is centred on the apex or nadir. The angle between the middle of the rolling section and the apex is charged once for the whole section. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, and loops high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A pause between two rolls or snaps on a loop is part of the same rolling section as the rolls on that loop, and the whole section must be centred about the apex or nadir. The pause is not scored separately: FCScore scores the rolls, snaps and pauses of the loop together as one window, under the roll centring downgrade (loop_roll_centre), and this key is only used to join the pause into it. The pads of the loop before and after the rolling section are not part of it.

    FCScore takes the whole rolling section of one loop as a single window: the rolls and snaps and the pauses between them, but not the loop flown either side of it. It reads the flight path elevation where the section starts and where it ends. The path falls through the top of a loop and rises through the bottom, so the average of the two elevations is zero when the section is centred about the apex or nadir, whatever the size and shape of the loop (round, P, Q or reversing) and however much of it the pilot uses. An error of 10° in where the roll sits on the loop is a 10° error in that average. FCScore charges its size once, at the end of the section, as an angle, so a roll centred early and one centred late cost the same. It is measured from the flown path, so a roll that misses the apex altogether is still charged for how far from it it was. Rolls and snaps on straight lines are not covered, and neither are loops whose roll fills the whole loop element, which have no apex to centre on. The extra deduction for flying part of a roll on a straight line is not measured here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Where a roll sits on a loop is easiest to judge when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where the position along the loop is hidden. It is also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side. The weighting does not depend on how much of the loop the roll uses. Large errors are counted in full.

> If there is a roll or rolls at the apex of the loop, it must be centred in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself. Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centred, it must be downgraded one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of the arc that it is off centre.
>
> [B.9.10.4](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Roll Rate Consistency {#roll_rate}

`roll_rate`

Checks that the roll rate is constant through each roll. The size of the variation in roll rate, compared with the average, is charged once for the roll. Small variations are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, and for short part-rolls that give less to judge.

??? note "Details"

    Rolls must be flown at a constant roll rate: any variance costs one point, for example slowing sharply for the last 45° of a 180° roll. Rolling turns are judged in the same way.

    FCScore measures the roll rate throughout each roll and calculates how much it varies as a fraction of its average. A steady roll scores zero, whatever its rate. The more the rate varies, the larger the downgrade. FCScore charges in proportion to the variation, not in whole points per occurrence.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting also grows with the amount of roll flown: a full roll or more counts fully, a half roll counts about half, because short rolls give the judge less to assess. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors.

> The penalty for varying the rate of roll is one (1) point per variation. Any stoppage in the aileron roll that could result in its being considered a hesitation roll, would hard zero (HZ) the figure.
>
> [B.9.23.1](#rb-rolls.rate)

> Each variation in the rate of roll is no more than a one (1) point deduction. Each stoppage of the rate of roll is a deduction of two (2) points.
>
> [B.9.3.6 d](#rb-turns.rolling_rate)

### Roll Pauses {#roll_excitation}

`roll_excitation`

Checks that the roll does not stop partway. The share of the roll for which the roll rate is close to zero, or reversed, is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    The rate of roll must not stop in a slow roll or a rolling turn, apart from a brief pause when changing roll direction, and each stoppage of the rate of roll in a rolling turn costs two points (B.9.3.6 d). A stoppage in an aileron roll that could be taken for a hesitation roll is a hard zero (B.9.23.1).

    FCScore counts the time during each roll in which the roll rate is effectively zero or reversed. A rate below about 1.5° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 3° per second counts as moving, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the roll's duration spent stopped, so a long hold costs more than a brief one.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> The penalty for varying the rate of roll is one (1) point per variation. Any stoppage in the aileron roll that could result in its being considered a hesitation roll, would hard zero (HZ) the figure.
>
> [B.9.23.1](#rb-rolls.rate)

> Each stoppage of the rate of turn is a deduction of two (2) points. … Each stoppage of the rate of roll is a deduction of two (2) points.
>
> [B.9.3.6 c, B.9.3.6 d](#rb-turns.rolling_stop)

### Loop Roundness {#radius}

`radius`

Checks that each loop is round, with a constant radius throughout. The variation of the radius within the loop, compared with its average, is charged once for the loop. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, high or wide in the box, and part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    Looping lines must have a constant radius. The judge divides the loop into quadrants, and any recognizable variation in the radius is downgraded by a maximum of two points per quadrant, depending on its size (B.9.10.5).

    FCScore fits a circle to the flown path of the loop in the plane of the loop and measures how much the aircraft's distance from the fitted centre varies, as a fraction of the average radius. A perfectly round loop scores zero, whatever its size, and the more the radius varies the larger the downgrade.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Shape errors are easiest to see when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where distortions are hidden. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter. Large errors are counted in full.

> A loop must have, by definition, a constant radius.
>
> [B.8.2.2 a](#rb-loops.radius)

> To better quantify deductions for irregularity of the radius of looping figures, the Judge divides the loop into quadrants. Any recognizable variation in the radius must be downgraded by a maximum of two (2) points per quadrant depending on the magnitude of the variation.
>
> [B.9.10.5](#rb-loops.radius_deductions)

### Flat Spots in Loops {#radius_excitation}

`radius_excitation`

Checks that the loop has no straight sections. The share of the loop for which the flight path is effectively straight is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when the loop is high or wide in the box, when the direction towards the loop centre lies along the line of sight, and for part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    Looping lines must have a constant radius, and where a roll is integrated into a loop any part of the roll flown on a straight line costs at least two points.

    FCScore watches the curvature of the flight path through the loop and counts the time during which it is effectively straight, or curving the wrong way. A local radius of about 1000 m or more counts as fully flat and about 500 m or less counts as curved, with values in between counting partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the loop's duration that is flat.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. These errors are easier to see when the direction from the aircraft towards the centre of the loop lies across the judge's line of sight, and harder when it lies along it. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter.

> A loop must have, by definition, a constant radius.
>
> [B.8.2.2 a](#rb-loops.radius)

> If there is a roll or rolls at the apex of the loop, it must be centred in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself. Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centred, it must be downgraded one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of the arc that it is off centre.
>
> [B.9.10.4](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Loop Rate of Turn {#curvature}

`curvature`

Checks that the loop keeps a steady rate of turn for its speed. The variation in the loop's curvature, compared with its average, is charged once for the loop. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when the loop is high or wide in the box, when the direction towards the loop centre lies along the line of sight, and for part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    Looping lines must have a constant radius, which means the aircraft has to turn at a steady rate for its speed, neither tightening nor opening up as it goes round.

    FCScore measures the rate of turn divided by the speed of travel (the curvature, which is one over the radius) throughout the loop and calculates how much it varies as a fraction of its average. Because it is based on how quickly the aircraft is turning for its speed, it picks up a tightening or opening of the loop early. The more the curvature varies, the larger the downgrade.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. These errors are easier to see when the direction from the aircraft towards the centre of the loop lies across the judge's line of sight, and harder when it lies along it. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter.

> A loop must have, by definition, a constant radius.
>
> [B.8.2.2 a](#rb-loops.radius)

### Spin Rotation Axis {#spin_rotation_axis}

`spin_rotation_axis`

Checks that the spin is a true autorotation. Time spent rotating about an axis too close to the fuselage line, below 25°, is charged. Small errors are discounted only for aircraft that are high or wide in the box, where the angle is harder to judge.

??? note "Details"

    A spin is a fully stalled autorotation. If the aircraft never stalls it cannot spin, and the figure is downgraded by four points (B.9.27.6). During autorotation the pitch attitude and the speed of rotation are not judging criteria, so only the type of rotation matters.

    FCScore measures the angle between the fuselage axis and the axis the aircraft is rotating about, from 15° after the break to 45° before the end of the rotation. Any period in which it is below 25° looks like a roll about the fuselage rather than an autorotation and is charged, according to how far below the limit it is and how large a share of the spin it covers. The 25° threshold is an FCScore way of detecting autorotation, not a number given in the rules. The charge rises to about 4 points when the rotation never looks like an autorotation, the CIVA deduction for a spin that never stalls.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The visibility factors are the aircraft's position in the box (errors are harder to judge high in the box or far to one side) and a fixed balancing factor. Large errors are counted in full.

> In all spins the marking criteria are: a) A clean breaking stall in horizontal flight. b) Fully stalled autorotation. c) Stopping on pre-stated heading. d) 90 degrees down, wings-level attitude after stopping on heading.
>
> [B.9.27.7](#rb-spins.definition)

> If the aircraft never stalls, it is apparent that it cannot spin, and a downgrade by four (4) points must be given.
>
> [B.9.27.6](#rb-spins.no_stall)

> Throughout the flick, the roll must be driven primarily by the rudder and autorotation must be seen to continue.
>
> [B.9.25.4](#rb-general.autorotation)

### Spin Nose Drop {#drop_pitch_rate}

`drop_pitch_rate`

Checks that the nose drops as the aircraft stalls into the spin. Time spent dropping slower than 6° per second in the first 15° of rotation is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: with the aircraft high or wide in the box, or directly above the judge.

??? note "Details"

    In a correct spin entry the nose of the glider drops and autorotation starts simultaneously around the longitudinal and vertical axes (B.9.27.2). A spin entered without a stall, for example a barrel roll or flick roll offered as a spin entry, is downgraded by four points (B.9.27.6).

    FCScore measures the nose-down pitch rate from the start of the spin until the first 15° of rotation is complete. Any period below 6° per second is charged, according to how far below it is and how large a share of that window it covers. The 6° per second figure is an FCScore threshold for a definite nose drop, not a number from the rules. A complete failure to drop the nose is charged about 4 points, the CIVA deduction for a spin that never stalls.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The nose drop is harder to see when the aircraft is directly above the judge, and when it is high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error. Large errors are counted in full.

> All spins start from horizontal flight. In order to spin, the aircraft must be completely stalled on a clearly visible horizontal line near its minimum airspeed. In a correct spin entry, the nose of the glider drops and autorotation starts simultaneously around the longitudinal and vertical axes.
>
> [B.9.27.2](#rb-spins.entry)

> If the aircraft never stalls, it is apparent that it cannot spin, and a downgrade by four (4) points must be given.
>
> [B.9.27.6](#rb-spins.no_stall)

### Spin Rotation Hesitation {#spin_excitation}

`spin_excitation`

Checks that the spin keeps rotating. The share of the spin for which the rotation rate is very low is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    Autorotation must continue throughout the spin. Early stopping of the autorotation followed by aileroning to the pre-stated heading costs one point for every 5° of aileroning (B.9.27.5).

    FCScore counts the time in each spin during which the rotation rate in the correct direction is close to zero or reversed. A rate below about 9° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 17° per second counts as rotating, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the spin's duration spent stopped.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> Be alert for early stopping of the stalled autorotation followed by "aileroning" to the pre-stated heading. In this case, a deduction of one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of "aileroning" must be applied.
>
> [B.9.27.5](#rb-spins.continue)

### Spin Exit Pitch Attitude {#spin_exit_pitch}

`spin_exit_pitch`

Checks that the aircraft ends the spin pointing vertically down in pitch. The full pitch angle error of the fuselage at the end of the spin is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    After the prescribed turns the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the pre-stated heading, and a 90° down, wings-level attitude must then be seen (B.9.27.4). Alignment errors cost one point for every 5°.

    FCScore takes the last point of the spin and charges the whole angle between the fuselage and the template downline in the pitch direction. It is an absolute measure at that point. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> 90 degrees down, wings-level attitude after stopping on heading.
>
> [B.9.27.7 d](#rb-spins.downline)

> After completion of the prescribed number of turns, the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the pre-stated heading, then a 90 degree down, wings-level attitude must be seen.
>
> [B.9.27.4](#rb-spins.stop)

### Spin Exit Sideways Lean {#spin_exit_yaw}

`spin_exit_yaw`

Checks that the aircraft ends the spin pointing vertically down, not leaning to the side. The full sideways angle error of the fuselage at the end of the spin is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    After the prescribed turns the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the pre-stated heading, and a 90° down, wings-level attitude must then be seen (B.9.27.4). Alignment errors cost one point for every 5°.

    FCScore takes the last point of the spin and charges the whole sideways angle between the fuselage and the template downline. It is an absolute measure at that point. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> After completion of the prescribed number of turns, the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the pre-stated heading, then a 90 degree down, wings-level attitude must be seen.
>
> [B.9.27.4](#rb-spins.stop)

> 90 degrees down, wings-level attitude after stopping on heading.
>
> [B.9.27.7 d](#rb-spins.downline)

### Snap Rotation Axis {#snap_rotation_axis}

`snap_rotation_axis`

Checks that the snap is a true autorotation rather than an axial roll. Time spent rotating about an axis too close to the fuselage line, below 10°, is charged. Small errors are discounted only for aircraft that are high or wide in the box, where the angle is harder to judge.

??? note "Details"

    A flick roll (snap) is an autorotation driven by the rudder, seen as a conical motion of the fuselage rather than a simple roll about the fuselage line (B.9.25.4). If the autorotation is not clearly seen the mark is downgraded by four points (B.9.25.2).

    FCScore measures the angle between the fuselage axis and the axis the aircraft is rotating about, from 15° after the start of the rotation to 90° before its end. Any period in which it is below 10° looks like an aileron roll and is charged, according to how far below the limit it is and how large a share of the snap it covers. The threshold is an FCScore way of detecting autorotation, not a number given in the rules. The charge rises to about 4 points when the rotation never looks like an autorotation, the CIVA deduction for a flick roll that was not properly initiated.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The visibility factors are the aircraft's position in the box (errors are harder to judge high in the box or far to one side) and a fixed balancing factor. Large errors are counted in full.

> When, or shortly after, the fuselage pitches the glider must be seen to yaw, initiating a stall of one wing and the rapid onset of autorotation.
>
> [B.9.25.3](#rb-snap_rolls.definition)

> Throughout the flick, the roll must be driven primarily by the rudder and autorotation must be seen to continue.
>
> [B.9.25.4](#rb-general.autorotation)

### Snap Rotation Hesitation {#snap_excitation}

`snap_excitation`

Checks that the snap keeps rotating. The share of the snap for which the rotation rate is low is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    Autorotation must continue throughout the snap. If it ceases before the end of the roll, one point is deducted for every 5° of rotation remaining, and if more than 45° remain the flick roll is awarded 0.0 (B.9.25.5). FCScore does not model that cut-off: an early stop is charged on a graded scale that reaches about 3 points when the snap is stopped throughout.

    FCScore counts the time in each snap during which the rotation rate in the correct direction is low. A rate below about 30° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 57° per second counts as rotating, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the snap's duration spent stopped.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> in this case, a deduction of one (1) point for each five (5) degrees of rotation remaining when the autorotation ceases must be made. If autorotation ends with more than 45 degrees of rotation remaining, even if the roll is completed with aileron, the flick roll is awarded a numerical zero (0.0).
>
> [B.9.25.5](#rb-snap_rolls.autorotation)

### Positive Snap Pitch Break {#pos_break_pr}

`pos_break_pr`

Checks that a positive snap starts with a clear pitch break. If the peak pitch rate in the first 15° of rotation never reaches 30° per second, the shortfall is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, or when it is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    To show a positive snap has been correctly initiated the judge must see a rapid and clearly visible pitch rotation in the nose up / tail down sense, followed by visible yaw and autorotation. If the required pitch change is not clearly seen, the mark is downgraded by four points (B.9.25.2).

    FCScore looks at the pitch rate over the first 15° of the rotation and takes its largest absolute value. If that peak never reaches 30° per second the shortfall is charged, up to about 4 points for no pitch break at all. The 30° per second figure is an FCScore threshold for a clear break, not a number from the rules, and only the peak counts.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Pitch rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error.

> The judge must see two things to determine that a flick roll has been correctly initiated: a) the aircraft must display a rapid and clearly visible change of pitch attitude to put the wing close to the stall, and b) autorotation must be initiated by use of the rudder. … However, if the required pitch change and/or actual autorotation are not clearly seen, the mark must be downgraded by four (4) points.
>
> [B.9.25.2](#rb-snap_rolls.break)

### Negative Snap Pitch Break {#neg_break_pr}

`neg_break_pr`

Checks that a negative snap starts with a clear pitch break. The peak pitch rate in the first 15° of rotation is compared with a 30° per second threshold and any shortfall is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, or when it is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A negative snap roll uses the same criteria as a positive one except that the nose and tail must initially move in the nose down / tail up sense, with a rapid and clearly visible pitch rotation. As for a positive snap, a pitch change that is not clearly seen is a four point downgrade (B.9.25.2, B.9.26.1).

    FCScore looks at the pitch rate over the first 15° of the rotation and compares its absolute value with a 30° per second threshold, charging any shortfall, up to about 4 points for no pitch break at all. The threshold is an FCScore value for a clear break, not a number from the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Pitch rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error.

> For negative flick rolls, all criteria stated for positive flick rolls apply … except that the aircraft is in a negative rather than positive angle-of-attack during autorotation.
>
> [B.9.26.1](#rb-snap_rolls.negative)

> The judge must see two things to determine that a flick roll has been correctly initiated: a) the aircraft must display a rapid and clearly visible change of pitch attitude to put the wing close to the stall, and b) autorotation must be initiated by use of the rudder. … However, if the required pitch change and/or actual autorotation are not clearly seen, the mark must be downgraded by four (4) points.
>
> [B.9.25.2](#rb-snap_rolls.break)

### Snap Exit Pitch Attitude {#snap_exit_pitch}

`snap_exit_pitch`

Checks that the aircraft returns to the correct pitch attitude after a snap on a vertical or 45° line. Only growth in the pitch error between the start and end of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    At the end of a flick roll the autorotation must stop as quickly as it started, followed immediately by the attitude that fits the underlying figure, and errors in the extent of rotation or the following attitude cost one point for every 5° (B.9.25.4).

    FCScore compares the fuselage pitch relative to the template at the first and last points of the snap and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the attitude closer to the template than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. It applies to snaps that do not finish on a horizontal line. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> autorotation must stop as quickly as it started, after the desired extent of roll, followed immediately by the adoption of the attitude that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. Downgrades for minor errors in the extent of rotation or the following flight path or attitude are penalised at the normal rate of 1 point per 5 degrees.
>
> [B.9.25.4](#rb-snap_rolls.exit)

### Snap Exit Yaw Attitude {#snap_exit_yaw}

`snap_exit_yaw`

Checks that the aircraft returns to the correct heading after a snap on a vertical or 45° line. Only growth in the yaw error between the start and end of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    At the end of a flick roll the autorotation must stop as quickly as it started, followed immediately by the attitude that fits the underlying figure, and errors in the extent of rotation or the following attitude cost one point for every 5° (B.9.25.4).

    FCScore compares the fuselage yaw relative to the template at the first and last points of the snap and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the attitude closer to the template than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. It applies to snaps that do not finish on a horizontal line. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> autorotation must stop as quickly as it started, after the desired extent of roll, followed immediately by the adoption of the attitude that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. Downgrades for minor errors in the extent of rotation or the following flight path or attitude are penalised at the normal rate of 1 point per 5 degrees.
>
> [B.9.25.4](#rb-snap_rolls.exit)

### Snap Exit Climb Angle {#snap_exit_climb}

`snap_exit_climb`

Checks that the flight path keeps its glide after a snap (flick roll) that finishes on a horizontal line. Only a change in the climb or descent angle between the start and end of the snap is charged, measured from the start angle limited to the bracket from level to 10° below the horizon. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    At the end of a flick roll the aircraft must immediately adopt the attitude and flight path that fit the underlying figure (B.9.25.4), and horizontal lines are judged on flight path, from level to 10° below the horizon. Failing to re-establish it costs one point for every 5°.

    FCScore compares the flight path angle to the horizontal at the first and last points of the snap, relative to the angle at the start of the snap (taken as no lower than level and no higher than 10° below the horizon), and charges any increase in the difference between them. A snap that leaves the path closer to that angle than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> autorotation must stop as quickly as it started, after the desired extent of roll, followed immediately by the adoption of the attitude that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. Downgrades for minor errors in the extent of rotation or the following flight path or attitude are penalised at the normal rate of 1 point per 5 degrees.
>
> [B.9.25.4](#rb-snap_rolls.exit)

> All lines are judged in relation to the true horizon and the Aerobatic Box axes. Horizontal lines are judged on flight path, not attitude.
>
> [B.8.1.1](#rb-lines.horizontal)

> Horizontal lines in glider aerobatics may be inclined between zero (0) and ten (10) degrees below the horizon. … Deviations above or below this bracket will be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.
>
> [4.5.1.3, B.8.1.2](#rb-gliders.glide_bracket)

### Snap Exit Heading {#snap_exit_heading}

`snap_exit_heading`

Checks that the heading returns to the box axis after a snap that finishes on a horizontal line. Only growth in the heading error between the start and end of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    At the end of a snap the aircraft must immediately adopt the attitude that fits the underlying figure, and on a horizontal line the heading must remain parallel to the box axis. Failing to re-establish it costs one point for every 5°.

    FCScore compares the fuselage heading relative to the template at the first and last points of the snap and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the heading closer to the template than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> autorotation must stop as quickly as it started, after the desired extent of roll, followed immediately by the adoption of the attitude that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. Downgrades for minor errors in the extent of rotation or the following flight path or attitude are penalised at the normal rate of 1 point per 5 degrees.
>
> [B.9.25.4](#rb-snap_rolls.exit)

> While maintaining a horizontal flight path, the aircraft's longitudinal axis must remain parallel to the X or Y axis. The deduction for deviation in either axis is one (1) point per five (5) degrees from the correct geometry.
>
> [B.8.1.3](#rb-lines.heading)

### Stall Turn Pivot Width {#width}

`width`

Checks that the aircraft pivots near its centre of gravity at the top of a stall turn. The sideways travel in the direction of the turn beyond an allowance is charged, ignoring downwind drift. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    The glider must pivot around a point that is not farther from its centre of gravity than its wingtip, and when the radius of the rotation is greater the downgrade is one point per half wingspan (B.9.5.2 f).

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft's centre of gravity moves sideways in the direction of the turn from the start of the stall turn, with movement from drifting downwind removed but upwind drift left in. The largest width beyond a fixed allowance is charged once. FCScore uses a fixed distance rather than your wingspan, so it approximates the wingspan-based rule, and it charges smoothly rather than in half-wingspan steps.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

    The results plot shows the sideways distance moved in metres with the allowance as a dashed line. The judged line follows the measurement up to the allowance and, beyond it, shows the visibility-reduced width that is charged.

> To avoid a deduction, it must pivot around a point which should not be farther away from its centre of gravity than its wingtip. When the radius of the rotation is greater, the downgrade is one (1) point per half wingspan.
>
> [B.9.5.2 f](#rb-stall_turns.pivot)

### Stall Turn Height Loss {#height}

`height`

Checks that the aircraft does not lose height through the pivot of a stall turn. How far below its highest point the aircraft is at the start and end of the stall turn, beyond an allowance, is charged. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    The glider must pivot around a point that is not farther from its centre of gravity than its wingtip, and when the radius of the rotation is greater the downgrade is one point per half wingspan (B.9.5.2 f).

    FCScore measures how far below the highest point of the stall turn the aircraft is at the first and last points of the stall turn element, and charges any height lost beyond a fixed allowance. FCScore uses a fixed distance rather than your wingspan, so it approximates the wingspan-based rule, and it charges smoothly rather than in half-wingspan steps.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

    The results plot shows how far the aircraft is below its highest point, in metres, with the allowance as dashed lines. The judged line follows the measurement inside the allowance and, beyond it, shows the visibility-reduced height loss that is charged.

> To avoid a deduction, it must pivot around a point which should not be farther away from its centre of gravity than its wingtip. When the radius of the rotation is greater, the downgrade is one (1) point per half wingspan.
>
> [B.9.5.2 f](#rb-stall_turns.pivot)

### Stall Turn Downline Yaw {#stallturn_exit_yaw}

`stallturn_exit_yaw`

Checks that the downline after a stall turn is not leaning sideways. The full sideways attitude error at the end of the line is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    After the pivot the aircraft must be established on a vertical downline, which like all vertical lines is judged on attitude, at one point per 5° of error.

    FCScore takes the last point of the line that follows the stall turn and charges the whole sideways angle between the fuselage and the template. It is an absolute measure at the end of the line. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Judging vertical lines is based on the attitude of the aircraft and not its flight path. When an aircraft's flight path, in a zero-wind condition, is exactly 90 degrees to the horizon, the wings are being held at the correct angle to produce no lift. The aircraft's attitude while in this condition (zero lift) defines the proper judging criterion for vertical attitude. This is called the zero-lift axis.
>
> [B.3.2.1](#rb-lines.vertical)

> To avoid a deduction, it must pivot around a point which should not be farther away from its centre of gravity than its wingtip. When the radius of the rotation is greater, the downgrade is one (1) point per half wingspan.
>
> [B.9.5.2 f](#rb-stall_turns.pivot)

### Stall Turn Downline Pitch {#stallturn_exit_pitch}

`stallturn_exit_pitch`

Checks that the downline after a stall turn is truly vertical in pitch. The full pitch attitude error at the end of the line is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    After the pivot the aircraft must be established on a vertical downline, which like all vertical lines is judged on attitude, at one point per 5° of error.

    FCScore takes the last point of the line that follows the stall turn and charges the whole pitch angle between the fuselage and the template. It is an absolute measure at the end of the line. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Judging vertical lines is based on the attitude of the aircraft and not its flight path. When an aircraft's flight path, in a zero-wind condition, is exactly 90 degrees to the horizon, the wings are being held at the correct angle to produce no lift. The aircraft's attitude while in this condition (zero lift) defines the proper judging criterion for vertical attitude. This is called the zero-lift axis.
>
> [B.3.2.1](#rb-lines.vertical)

> To avoid a deduction, it must pivot around a point which should not be farther away from its centre of gravity than its wingtip. When the radius of the rotation is greater, the downgrade is one (1) point per half wingspan.
>
> [B.9.5.2 f](#rb-stall_turns.pivot)

### Tailslide Sideways Lean {#tailslide_yaw}

`tailslide_yaw`

Checks that the aircraft does not lean sideways during a tailslide. Only growth in the sideways lean of the fuselage is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    All the criteria of the stall turn apply to a tailslide, so the vertical lines are judged on the zero-lift axis and any deviation from vertical costs one point for every 5° (B.9.6.1, B.9.5.2 b). The wings must stay level throughout the slide and the fall through (B.9.6.4).

    FCScore measures the lean of the fuselage sideways relative to the template throughout the tailslide and charges each increase in the absolute angle; a decrease is free. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> All the criteria of the Stall Turn apply to this figure except, of course, for the manoeuvre at the top of the vertical climb. … Any deviation from vertical, either up or down, will result in a deduction of one (1) point per five (5) degrees from the zero-lift axis. … Wings should stay level with the horizon throughout and not drop during the slide or the fall through.
>
> [B.9.6.1, B.9.5.2 b, B.9.6.4](#rb-tailslides.lean)

### Tailslide Exit Pitch {#tailslide_exit_pitch}

`tailslide_exit_pitch`

Checks that the aircraft finishes the tailslide pointing vertically down in pitch. The full pitch attitude error at the end of the tailslide is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    After the backwards slide the aircraft must tip over and fall through to a diving position, around the lateral axis only, at one point for every 5° of movement about another axis (B.9.6.2). The nose may swing back past the vertical, which is neither downgraded nor required (B.9.6.3).

    FCScore takes the last point of the tailslide and charges the whole pitch angle between the fuselage and the template. It is an absolute measure at that point, so a swing past the vertical that has settled by then is not charged. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Following the slide backwards, the aircraft must then tip over and fall through to a diving position. The tipping over must be around the lateral axis only. Any movement around another axis is downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees. … Often the nose will swing back or "pendulum" past the vertical after falling through. The figure is not to be downgraded for this, nor downgraded if it does not happen.
>
> [B.9.6.2, B.9.6.3](#rb-tailslides.recovery)

### Tailslide Stop {#tailslide_stop}

`tailslide_stop`

Checks that the aircraft comes to a stop at the top of the vertical line before it slides back. The vertical speed left at the end of the upline is charged once. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    In a tailslide the aircraft climbs vertically and stops before sliding backwards, with the backwards slide beginning when upward motion ceases.

    FCScore takes the last point of the line before the tailslide and charges the absolute vertical speed there. A larger speed means the aircraft was still climbing, or already falling, instead of being stopped. The downgrade scale is an FCScore value; the rules do not set a speed limit.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> In summary, the aircraft should make a smooth and steady transition up to vertical flight, the wings should stay level in relation to the horizon, and the aircraft should come to a complete stop in this attitude.
>
> [B.9.6.7](#rb-tailslides.definition)

### Tailslide Slide Distance {#tailslide_drop}

`tailslide_drop`

Checks that the aircraft slides backwards a visible distance. A slide shorter than 0.3 m is charged, up to about 4 points for no slide. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    At the point where the glider stops it must slide backwards a visible amount; the key is that the slide is visible. If the tailslide does not move backwards the deduction is 4 points (B.9.6.1).

    FCScore adds up the distance travelled backwards through the tailslide and charges any shortfall below 0.3 m. The rules do not give a distance for a visible slide, so 0.3 m is an FCScore value. The charge rises with the shortfall to about 4 points when there is no slide at all, rather than applying the fixed deduction.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the point when the aircraft stops, it must slide backwards a visible amount (the key here is "a visible amount"). If a tailslide does not move backwards the reduction is -4,0 p.
>
> [B.9.6.1](#rb-tailslides.slide)

### Sequence Entry Climb {#seqstart_entry_climb}

`seqstart_entry_climb`

Checks the climb angle before the first figure. The angle outside the bracket from level to 10° below the horizon at the start of the window, just before the figure, is charged in full. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Figures begin in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged before the first figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure level and aligned and does not dive, climb or bank into it. A glider's horizontal line may be inclined between 0 and 10° below the horizon (B.8.1.2).

    FCScore takes the sample one second before the start of the first element of the figure and charges the angle by which the flight path is outside the bracket from level to 10° below the horizon. It is an absolute measure because nothing earlier has been charged. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the entry and exit of every figure the aircraft longitudinal axis must be exactly aligned with either the main or secondary axis of the Aerobatic Box. Any angular deviations visible to the judge must be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.
>
> [B.6.1.1](#rb-general.figure_start)

> All lines are judged in relation to the true horizon and the Aerobatic Box axes. Horizontal lines are judged on flight path, not attitude.
>
> [B.8.1.1](#rb-lines.horizontal)

> Horizontal lines in glider aerobatics may be inclined between zero (0) and ten (10) degrees below the horizon. … Deviations above or below this bracket will be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.
>
> [4.5.1.3, B.8.1.2](#rb-gliders.glide_bracket)

### Sequence Entry Climb Drift {#seqstart_climb}

`seqstart_climb`

Checks the climb angle stays correct before the first figure. Only growth in the error over the window next to the figure is charged, so a correction back towards the template is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Figures begin in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged before the first figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure level and aligned and does not dive, climb or bank into it. A glider's horizontal line may be inclined between 0 and 10° below the horizon (B.8.1.2).

    FCScore measures how the angle between the flight path and the horizontal changes over the last second of the line before the figure, relative to the angle at the start of the window (taken as no lower than level and no higher than 10° below the horizon), and charges each increase in the difference; a decrease is free. An error already present at the start of the window is charged by the matching check at that point, not again here. The window ends where the figure starts and moves with it, so the error cannot be moved out of the score by placing the start of the figure later. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the entry and exit of every figure the aircraft longitudinal axis must be exactly aligned with either the main or secondary axis of the Aerobatic Box. Any angular deviations visible to the judge must be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.
>
> [B.6.1.1](#rb-general.figure_start)

> All lines are judged in relation to the true horizon and the Aerobatic Box axes. Horizontal lines are judged on flight path, not attitude.
>
> [B.8.1.1](#rb-lines.horizontal)

> Horizontal lines in glider aerobatics may be inclined between zero (0) and ten (10) degrees below the horizon. … Deviations above or below this bracket will be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.
>
> [4.5.1.3, B.8.1.2](#rb-gliders.glide_bracket)

### Sequence Entry Heading {#seqstart_entry_heading}

`seqstart_entry_heading`

Checks the heading before the first figure. The error at the start of the window, just before the figure, is charged in full. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Figures begin in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged before the first figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure level and aligned and does not dive, climb or bank into it.

    FCScore takes the sample one second before the start of the first element of the figure and charges the whole angle between the fuselage and the template heading in the horizontal plane, which measures the nose rather than the flight path. It is an absolute measure because nothing earlier has been charged. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the entry and exit of every figure the aircraft longitudinal axis must be exactly aligned with either the main or secondary axis of the Aerobatic Box. Any angular deviations visible to the judge must be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.
>
> [B.6.1.1](#rb-general.figure_start)

> While maintaining a horizontal flight path, the aircraft's longitudinal axis must remain parallel to the X or Y axis. The deduction for deviation in either axis is one (1) point per five (5) degrees from the correct geometry.
>
> [B.8.1.3](#rb-lines.heading)

### Sequence Entry Wings Level {#seqstart_entry_roll}

`seqstart_entry_roll`

Checks the roll angle before the first figure. The error at the start of the window, just before the figure, is charged in full. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    Figures begin in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged before the first figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure level and aligned and does not dive, climb or bank into it.

    FCScore takes the sample one second before the start of the first element of the figure and charges the whole difference between the aircraft's roll angle and the template attitude. It is an absolute measure because nothing earlier has been charged. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the entry and exit of every figure the aircraft longitudinal axis must be exactly aligned with either the main or secondary axis of the Aerobatic Box. Any angular deviations visible to the judge must be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.
>
> [B.6.1.1](#rb-general.figure_start)

> For deviations from the correct geometry (plane of flight, direction of flight, angle of bank) and for deviations from the proper flight path or the proper attitude (as appropriate), the mark will be reduced by 1 point per 5 degrees of deviation.
>
> [4.5.1.1](#rb-general.angle_rule)
