## Positioning (box) downgrades

### Box Ceiling {#top}

`top`

Checks that the figure stays below the top of the aerobatic box. The distance above the ceiling, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted. The deduction is not taken off this figure: it is added to the sequence's Positioning score.

??? note "Details"

    The upper height limit is 1200 m over datum (3.9.1.1). When a height measuring device is used a penalty of 70 points is given if the first figure is started above the limit or exceeds it, and there is no penalty for exceeding it in a later figure (4.4.1.1 a). The box ceiling is 1200 m for both categories.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is above the ceiling of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch above is charged in proportion to how far above it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules apply a fixed contest penalty per figure rather than a graded deduction, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement. The deduction does not reduce this figure's score. FCScore adds up the box deductions of all the figures of the sequence into one sequence-level Positioning mark, from 10 down to 0, and weights it with the schedule's Positioning K factor, as the judges' mark is weighted. The mark is continuous: FCScore does not round it to the steps the judges use. A schedule with no Positioning K factor, such as a Freestyle programme, keeps the deduction on the figure instead.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

> When an HMD is used, a penalty of 70 points is given if the first figure is started above 1200 m or this limit is exceeded in the course of the first figure.
>
> [4.4.1.1 a](#rb-box.ceiling)

> The following height limitations have been determined for all contest flights: a) Upper limit: 1200 m (over datum) … c) Lower limit: 200 m (over datum) d) Disqualification height: 100m (over datum)
>
> [3.9.1.1](#rb-box.heights)

### Right Box Boundary {#right}

`right`

Checks that the figure stays inside the the right boundary of the aerobatic box. The distance outside the boundary, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted. The deduction is not taken off this figure: it is added to the sequence's Positioning score.

??? note "Details"

    The performance zone is a marked area of 1000 x 1000 m. Excursions outside it, plus a 50 m tolerance, are registered by an electronic tracking system and the time flown outside is penalised by 2 points per second (4.4.2.1). FCScore measures from the boundary itself, without the 50 m tolerance.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is outside the right boundary of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch outside is charged in proportion to how far out it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules penalise the time spent outside the zone rather than deducting from the figure mark, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement. The deduction does not reduce this figure's score. FCScore adds up the box deductions of all the figures of the sequence into one sequence-level Positioning mark, from 10 down to 0, and weights it with the schedule's Positioning K factor, as the judges' mark is weighted. The mark is continuous: FCScore does not round it to the steps the judges use. A schedule with no Positioning K factor, such as a Freestyle programme, keeps the deduction on the figure instead.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

> The performance zone will be a clearly and distinctly marked area of 1000 x 1000 m, the central point of which will be the intersection of the axes.
>
> [3.4.1.1](#rb-box.limits)

> Excursions outside the performance zone (plus 50 m tolerance) will be registered by the electronic tracking system. The time flown outside the performance zone is penalised by 2 points per second.
>
> [4.4.2.1](#rb-box.boundary_penalty)

FCScore adds up the box deductions of all the figures of the sequence into one sequence-level Positioning mark, from 10 down to 0, and weights it with the schedule's Positioning K factor, as the judges' mark is weighted. The mark is continuous: FCScore does not round it to the steps the judges use. A schedule with no Positioning K factor, such as a Freestyle programme, keeps the deduction on the figure instead.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

> The performance zone will be a clearly and distinctly marked area of 1000 x 1000 m, the central point of which will be the intersection of the axes.
>
> [3.4.1.1](#rb-box.limits)

> Excursions outside the performance zone (plus 50 m tolerance) will be registered by the electronic tracking system. The time flown outside the performance zone is penalised by 2 points per second.
>
> [4.4.2.1](#rb-box.boundary_penalty)

### Back Box Boundary {#back}

`back`

Checks that the figure stays inside the back boundary of the aerobatic box. The distance beyond the boundary, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted. The deduction is not taken off this figure: it is added to the sequence's Positioning score.

??? note "Details"

    The performance zone is a marked area of 1000 x 1000 m. Excursions outside it, plus a 50 m tolerance, are registered by an electronic tracking system and the time flown outside is penalised by 2 points per second (4.4.2.1). FCScore measures from the boundary itself, without the 50 m tolerance. A figure flown too far away to be marked correctly also loses 2 points.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is beyond the back boundary of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch outside is charged in proportion to how far out it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules penalise the time spent outside the zone rather than deducting from the figure mark, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement. The deduction does not reduce this figure's score. FCScore adds up the box deductions of all the figures of the sequence into one sequence-level Positioning mark, from 10 down to 0, and weights it with the schedule's Positioning K factor, as the judges' mark is weighted. The mark is continuous: FCScore does not round it to the steps the judges use. A schedule with no Positioning K factor, such as a Freestyle programme, keeps the deduction on the figure instead.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

    The results plot shows the distance from the judge with the back boundary as a dashed line. The judged line follows the measurement inside the boundary and, beyond it, shows the visibility-reduced distance that is charged.

> The performance zone will be a clearly and distinctly marked area of 1000 x 1000 m, the central point of which will be the intersection of the axes.
>
> [3.4.1.1](#rb-box.limits)

> Should a competitor fly a figure at a location, inside or outside the performance zone, such that the accuracy of the flight path or attitude cannot reasonably be determined, a downgrade of 2 points should be applied for each element of the figure that cannot be properly assessed.
>
> [B.4.1.2](#rb-box.scorability)

`front`

Checks that the figure stays behind the front boundary of the aerobatic box. The distance in front of the boundary, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted. The deduction is not taken off this figure: it is added to the sequence's Positioning score.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is in front of the front boundary of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch outside is charged in proportion to how far out it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules penalise the time spent outside the zone rather than deducting from the figure mark, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement. The deduction does not reduce this figure's score. FCScore adds up the box deductions of all the figures of the sequence into one sequence-level Positioning mark, from 10 down to 0, and weights it with the schedule's Positioning K factor, as the judges' mark is weighted. The mark is continuous: FCScore does not round it to the steps the judges use. A schedule with no Positioning K factor, such as a Freestyle programme, keeps the deduction on the figure instead.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

    The results plot shows the distance from the judge with the front boundary as a dashed line. The judged line follows the measurement inside the boundary and, beyond it, shows the visibility-reduced distance that is charged.

> The performance zone will be a clearly and distinctly marked area of 1000 x 1000 m, the central point of which will be the intersection of the axes.
>
> [3.4.1.1](#rb-box.limits)

> Excursions outside the performance zone (plus 50 m tolerance) will be registered by the electronic tracking system. The time flown outside the performance zone is penalised by 2 points per second.

### Box Floor {#btm}

`btm`

Checks that the figure stays above the floor of the aerobatic box. The distance below the floor, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged heavily. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted. The deduction is not taken off this figure: it is added to the sequence's Positioning score.

??? note "Details"

    The lower height limit is 200 m over datum. A figure flown, or partly flown, below it receives 70 penalty points, and flying the programme below 100 m over datum is disqualified (4.4.1.1). The box floor is 200 m for both categories.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is below the floor of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch below is charged in proportion to how far below it is and for how much of the figure's duration, on a steeper scale than the other box limits. The rules apply fixed contest penalties rather than a graded deduction, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement. The deduction does not reduce this figure's score. FCScore adds up the box deductions of all the figures of the sequence into one sequence-level Positioning mark, from 10 down to 0, and weights it with the schedule's Positioning K factor, as the judges' mark is weighted. The mark is continuous: FCScore does not round it to the steps the judges use. A schedule with no Positioning K factor, such as a Freestyle programme, keeps the deduction on the figure instead.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

> A competitor flying a figure or part of a figure lower than 200 m (over datum) will receive 70 penalty points for this figure. A competitor flying their programme lower than 100 m (over datum) will be disqualified for this flight.
>
> [4.4.1.1](#rb-box.floor)

> The following height limitations have been determined for all contest flights: a) Upper limit: 1200 m (over datum) … c) Lower limit: 200 m (over datum) d) Disqualification height: 100m (over datum)
>
> [3.9.1.1](#rb-box.heights)

## Inter-element downgrades

### Loop Radius Matching {#inter.loop_radius}

`inter.loop_radius`

Checks that the looping lines in a figure that must have matching radii do match. Each radius is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    All the part-loops that are drawn as round elements in a figure must have the same radius, except in double humpty-bumps, and part-loops drawn as corners need not match other loops, except in combinations of lines (Family 3) and hesitation loops, which keep a regular shape (B.8.2.2 c, d). CIVA-G gives no standard deduction for a mismatch.

    FCScore takes the radius of each looping line the figure requires to match and compares each with the previous one, rather than with the first, charging in proportion to how many times larger one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the size. Whether each loop is round is judged by Loop Roundness.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> For any one figure having several internal part-loops depicted as round elements, all such part-loops shall have the same radius – with exception for all of family 8.8 figures (double humpty-bumps) for which the radius of the second part-loop is not required to match the radius of the first one.
>
> [B.8.2.2 c](#rb-loops.matching_radii)

> The radius of any part-loop depicted as a corner angle is not required to match the radius of any other part-loop in the same figure – with exception for all of Family 3 (combinations of lines) and Family 7.4 (hesitation loops) figures, which must keep a regular geometrical shape.
>
> [B.8.2.2 d](#rb-loops.corner_radii)

### Line Length Matching {#inter.line_length}

`inter.line_length`

Checks that lines that must be of equal length in a figure are. Each length is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    Interior lines do not have to be equal unless the figure says so, as in Family 3 and the square and octagon loops. Where equal lengths are required, a visible variation costs one point and a variation of 1:2 or more costs two points, with the first line flown as the basis, and the absence of one of the lines before or after a roll costs one additional point (B.8.1.11, B.8.1.12). Flick rolls need not be centred on an interior line (B.8.1.8), so a line on which every roll is a flick roll is not subject to the equal length rule.

    FCScore takes the length of each line the figure requires to match and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the length. A line on which every roll is a flick roll (snap) is left out of the comparison. FCScore's scale is smooth rather than in the rulebook's steps.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> If within a figure two or more lines must be of the same length, an observed variation is penalised by reducing the mark in the following manner: … a) a visible variation - one (1) point deduction … b) if the lengths vary by 1:2 or more - two (2) points deduction.
>
> [B.8.1.11](#rb-lines.length_penalty)

> The basis for judging line lengths is the first line flown. The absence of one of the lines before or after a roll is penalised by one (1) additional point.
>
> [B.8.1.12](#rb-lines.length_basis)

> In gliders, the entry airspeeds for positive and negative flick rolls lie in a relatively narrow bracket. Pilots must be free, therefore, to determine the point on the line where they start the flick roll. Because of this, no deduction will be made for flick rolls not centred on an interior line.
>
> [B.8.1.8](#rb-gliders.flick_centring)

### Roll Rate Matching {#inter.roll_rate}

`inter.roll_rate`

Checks that the rolls within one roll combination are flown at the same roll rate. Each rate is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    The rate of roll and the rhythm of the hesitations of a hesitation roll must be constant throughout (B.9.24.2). CIVA-G gives no deduction for rates that differ, so this charge is an FCScore approximation, following the hesitation roll rule most closely.

    FCScore takes the roll rate of each roll within a roll combination on the same line and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times faster one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the rate. FCScore groups rolls by the figure definition rather than by the rule, so check the rulebook for your figure. Whether the rate is steady within one roll is judged by Roll Rate Consistency.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> The rate of the roll and the rhythm of the hesitations must be constant throughout with the aircraft projecting the pre-stated plane and direction of flight.
>
> [B.9.24.2](#rb-rolls.hesitation_rate)

### Pause Duration Matching {#inter.point_duration}

`inter.point_duration`

Checks that the pauses between the rolls or points of a roll combination last the same time. Each duration is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    In a hesitation roll the pauses must be of identical duration, and a pause that is not recognizable is a hard zero (B.9.24.3). Unlinked rolls must also show a brief but perceptible pause between them (B.9.22.3 b). CIVA-G gives no deduction for pauses that differ, so this charge is an FCScore approximation.

    FCScore takes the duration of each pause in a roll combination on the same line and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the duration.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> The pauses will be of identical duration. Each pause of a hesitation roll must be clearly recognizable in every case … If a pause is not recognizable to a judge, the figure is marked a Hard Zero (HZ).
>
> [B.9.24.3](#rb-rolls.hesitation_pause)

> They must have a brief but perceptible pause between them, and they are to be flown in the same direction of rotation.
>
> [B.9.22.3 b](#rb-rolls.unlinked_pause)

### Roll Position On Line {#inter.pad_length}

`inter.pad_length`

Checks that a roll is centred on its line, with equal lengths of line before and after it. The two lengths are compared and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    Whenever an aileron roll or hesitation roll is placed on an interior line, the lengths of the two parts of the line before and after the roll must be equal (B.8.1.8), with the same penalties as other equal-length lines: one point for a visible variation and two points for a variation of 1:2 or more (B.8.1.11). Flick rolls need not be centred, because the entry speeds of glider flick rolls lie in a narrow bracket and pilots must be free to choose where to start them.

    FCScore compares the length of line before the roll with the length after, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A roll that is perfectly centred scores zero, whatever the length of the line. A line on which every roll is a flick roll (snap) is left out of the comparison, so a flick can sit anywhere on its line. A line that also has an aileron or hesitation roll is still compared, so those rolls must still be centred.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> Whenever an aileron roll or hesitation roll is placed on an interior line, the lengths of the two parts of the line before and after the roll must be equal.
>
> [B.8.1.8](#rb-lines.length_equal)

> If within a figure two or more lines must be of the same length, an observed variation is penalised by reducing the mark in the following manner: … a) a visible variation - one (1) point deduction … b) if the lengths vary by 1:2 or more - two (2) points deduction.
>
> [B.8.1.11](#rb-lines.length_penalty)

> In gliders, the entry airspeeds for positive and negative flick rolls lie in a relatively narrow bracket. Pilots must be free, therefore, to determine the point on the line where they start the flick roll. Because of this, no deduction will be made for flick rolls not centred on an interior line.
>
> [B.8.1.8](#rb-gliders.flick_centring)

## Sequence-level score

### Positioning {#presentation}

`presentation`

The sequence positioning mark for glider sequences. FCScore estimates it from the box deductions of all the figures, added up and taken off 10.

??? note "Details"

    In CIVA-G the positioning of the figures is marked by the judges (25K in the Unlimited programmes, 20K for Advanced), and where an electronic tracking system is in use a further 15K is given for the aircraft's position. Each judge combines the 'Pos' annotations into one sequence positioning mark, half a mark for each 'somewhat' non-optimal figure and a full mark for each 'considerably' non-optimal figure, and may revise it by up to one point.

    FCScore gives one positioning score for both: it adds up the box deductions of every figure (how far each figure strays outside the performance zone, measured as the box downgrades describe) and takes the total off 10, weighted by one K factor, the sum of the judges' and the electronic marks: 40K for Unlimited and 35K for Advanced (FCScore's score is closer to the tracking mark than to the judges' placement). The judges' 'Pos' annotations, the symmetry of the sequence and the revision are not modelled.

    The score is 10 minus the total of the figures' box deductions, with a lowest score of 0, and it is weighted by the schedule's Positioning K factor like an extra figure. A missing or failed figure adds nothing, because it already scores 0. The score is continuous, not rounded to the half points the judges use. A schedule with no Positioning K factor, such as a Freestyle programme, has no Positioning score and its figures keep their own box deductions.

> Positioning refers to the 3D placement of each figure relative to the performance zone and to the judges.
>
> [4.1.5.1](#rb-positioning.marking)

> At the end of the sequence the annotations in the “Pos” column shall be used by each judge to determine a sequence positioning downgrade based primarily on these recorded observations. Each single letter is taken as equivalent to a half mark and each double letter equivalent to a full mark downgrade. The Judge is entitled to revise his final positioning mark up or down by a maximum of 1 point if he considers there were other relevant factors which should be taken into account to reduce or increase the downgrade.
>
> [4.1.5.7](#rb-positioning.downgrade)

> Coefficients for the Programmes “UNG” (Programmes 1, 3, 2, 4, 5 and 6): Positioning (Electronic tracking system in use) 15K, Positioning (marked by Judges only) 25K. Coefficients for the Programmes “ADG”: Positioning (Electronic tracking system in use) 15K, Positioning (marked by Judges only) 20K.
>
> [2.3.4](#rb-positioning.k_factor)

> Positioning refers to the placement of the figures in relation to the main and secondary axes of the performance zone. Additionally, positioning relates to the placement of each figure at its optimum distance from the judges, taking into account the height of the glider and the nature of the figure being flown. Lastly, positioning also refers to the symmetrical placement of the entire sequence in relation to the lateral (secondary) axis of the performance zone.
>
> [B.10.1.2](#rb-positioning.optimal)

Coefficients for the Programmes “ADG”: Positioning (Electronic tracking system in use) 15K, Positioning (marked by Judges only) 20K.

### 4.4.1.1 {#rb-box.floor}

`box.floor`

> A competitor flying a figure or part of a figure lower than 200 m (over datum) will receive 70 penalty points for this figure. A competitor flying their programme lower than 100 m (over datum) will be disqualified for this flight.

### 4.4.1.1 a {#rb-box.ceiling}

`box.ceiling`

> When an HMD is used, a penalty of 70 points is given if the first figure is started above 1200 m or this limit is exceeded in the course of the first figure.

### 4.4.2.1 {#rb-box.boundary_penalty}

`box.boundary_penalty`

> Excursions outside the performance zone (plus 50 m tolerance) will be registered by the electronic tracking system. The time flown outside the performance zone is penalised by 2 points per second.

### 4.5.1.1 {#rb-general.angle_rule}

`general.angle_rule`

> For deviations from the correct geometry (plane of flight, direction of flight, angle of bank) and for deviations from the proper flight path or the proper attitude (as appropriate), the mark will be reduced by 1 point per 5 degrees of deviation.

### 4.5.1.3, B.8.1.2 {#rb-gliders.glide_bracket}

`gliders.glide_bracket`

> Horizontal lines in glider aerobatics may be inclined between zero (0) and ten (10) degrees below the horizon. … Deviations above or below this bracket will be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.

### 4.5.1.7 {#rb-general.corrections}

`general.corrections`

> Over-rotating a roll and rolling the wings back again must be penalised by 1 point per 5 degrees of over-rotation, even if the correct geometry is resumed afterwards, no matter how quickly the correction is made.

### B.10.1.2 {#rb-positioning.optimal}

`positioning.optimal`

> Positioning refers to the placement of the figures in relation to the main and secondary axes of the performance zone. Additionally, positioning relates to the placement of each figure at its optimum distance from the judges, taking into account the height of the glider and the nature of the figure being flown. Lastly, positioning also refers to the symmetrical placement of the entire sequence in relation to the lateral (secondary) axis of the performance zone.

### B.3.1.1 {#rb-general.flight_path}

`general.flight_path`

> Think of the aircraft condensed into a single dot and watch the path this dot takes through the sky. This is the flight path, or track, of the aircraft's centre of gravity.

### B.3.2.1 {#rb-lines.vertical}

`lines.vertical`

> Judging vertical lines is based on the attitude of the aircraft and not its flight path. When an aircraft's flight path, in a zero-wind condition, is exactly 90 degrees to the horizon, the wings are being held at the correct angle to produce no lift. The aircraft's attitude while in this condition (zero lift) defines the proper judging criterion for vertical attitude. This is called the zero-lift axis.

### B.3.3.1, B.3.3.2 {#rb-lines.diagonal}

`lines.diagonal`

> This is the vertical attitude plus or minus 45 degrees. … These changes in the flight path angle must also be ignored when judging 45 degree lines. The prescribed deduction is one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation from the correct geometry (0.5 points per 2.5 degrees).

### B.4.1.1 {#rb-general.grading}

`general.grading`

> It should be assumed that a competitor is going to fly a perfect figure, so a Judge starts with a mark of 10. As the figure is performed, the Judge then begins to find faults (if any) with what he or she sees and starts downgrading as the figure progresses.

### B.4.1.2 {#rb-box.scorability}

`box.scorability`

> Should a competitor fly a figure at a location, inside or outside the performance zone, such that the accuracy of the flight path or attitude cannot reasonably be determined, a downgrade of 2 points should be applied for each element of the figure that cannot be properly assessed.

### B.6.1.1 {#rb-general.figure_start}

`general.figure_start`

> At the entry and exit of every figure the aircraft longitudinal axis must be exactly aligned with either the main or secondary axis of the Aerobatic Box. Any angular deviations visible to the judge must be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.

### B.7.1.5 {#rb-general.wind_correction}

`general.wind_correction`

> A common flight mode is to crab into the wind as done in navigational flight. … The downside to this approach is that if the aircraft longitudinal axis is detected by the Judge to be at an angle to the competition axis (main or secondary), one (1) point per five (5) degrees must be deducted.

### B.8.1.1 {#rb-lines.horizontal}

`lines.horizontal`

> All lines are judged in relation to the true horizon and the Aerobatic Box axes. Horizontal lines are judged on flight path, not attitude.

### B.8.1.11 {#rb-lines.length_penalty}

`lines.length_penalty`

> If within a figure two or more lines must be of the same length, an observed variation is penalised by reducing the mark in the following manner: … a) a visible variation - one (1) point deduction … b) if the lengths vary by 1:2 or more - two (2) points deduction.

### B.8.1.12 {#rb-lines.length_basis}

`lines.length_basis`

> The basis for judging line lengths is the first line flown. The absence of one of the lines before or after a roll is penalised by one (1) additional point.

### B.8.1.3 {#rb-lines.heading}

`lines.heading`

> While maintaining a horizontal flight path, the aircraft's longitudinal axis must remain parallel to the X or Y axis. The deduction for deviation in either axis is one (1) point per five (5) degrees from the correct geometry.

### B.8.1.8 {#rb-gliders.flick_centring}

`gliders.flick_centring`

> In gliders, the entry airspeeds for positive and negative flick rolls lie in a relatively narrow bracket. Pilots must be free, therefore, to determine the point on the line where they start the flick roll. Because of this, no deduction will be made for flick rolls not centred on an interior line.

### B.8.1.8 {#rb-lines.length_equal}

`lines.length_equal`

> Whenever an aileron roll or hesitation roll is placed on an interior line, the lengths of the two parts of the line before and after the roll must be equal.

### B.8.2.2 a {#rb-loops.radius}

`loops.radius`

> A loop must have, by definition, a constant radius.

### B.8.2.2 c {#rb-loops.matching_radii}

`loops.matching_radii`

> For any one figure having several internal part-loops depicted as round elements, all such part-loops shall have the same radius – with exception for all of family 8.8 figures (double humpty-bumps) for which the radius of the second part-loop is not required to match the radius of the first one.

### B.8.2.2 d {#rb-loops.corner_radii}

`loops.corner_radii`

> The radius of any part-loop depicted as a corner angle is not required to match the radius of any other part-loop in the same figure – with exception for all of Family 3 (combinations of lines) and Family 7.4 (hesitation loops) figures, which must keep a regular geometrical shape.

### B.9.10.1 {#rb-loops.crosswind}

`loops.crosswind`

> All full loops must appear perfectly round to the Judge. This means that they must be wind corrected to have a constant radius. This wind correction is only with regards to the roundness of the loop and not for the effect of any crosswind on the figure.

### B.9.10.2 {#rb-gliders.loop_lines}

`gliders.loop_lines`

> In glider aerobatics, the entry and exit lines of the loop may be inclined 0 to 10 degrees below the horizon and the inclination may be different for entry and exit lines within the above tolerances

### B.9.10.3 {#rb-loops.crab_wings}

`loops.crab_wings`

> Loops must be flown with no visible crabbing and wings must be level at all times. The one (1) point for every five (5) degrees rule holds for both these cases.

### B.9.10.4 {#rb-loops.integrated_rolls}

`loops.integrated_rolls`

> If there is a roll or rolls at the apex of the loop, it must be centred in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself. Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centred, it must be downgraded one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of the arc that it is off centre.

### B.9.10.5 {#rb-loops.radius_deductions}

`loops.radius_deductions`

> To better quantify deductions for irregularity of the radius of looping figures, the Judge divides the loop into quadrants. Any recognizable variation in the radius must be downgraded by a maximum of two (2) points per quadrant depending on the magnitude of the variation.

### B.9.2.2, B.9.2.5 a {#rb-turns.entry_bank}

`turns.entry_bank`

> This must be a roll of 60 degrees, it must be performed on the entry heading, and the aircraft must maintain a constant glide (0 to 10 degrees below the horizon). … The angle of bank established by the initial rolling manoeuvre must be exactly 60 degrees. Any deviation is a one (1) point deduction for every five (5) degrees.

### B.9.2.3, B.9.2.5 b {#rb-turns.bank}

`turns.bank`

> The turn must maintain 60 degrees of bank throughout. … The angle of bank, once established, must remain constant. Any deviation is a one (1) point deduction for every five (5) degrees of deviation.

### B.9.2.5 d, B.9.3.6 b {#rb-turns.altitude}

`turns.altitude`

> The aircraft must maintain a constant glide (0 to 10 degrees below the horizon) throughout the figure. Any deviation above or below is one (1) point for every five (5) degrees. … Variations from the constant glide (0 to 10 degrees below the horizon) are deducted by one (1) point per five (5) degrees.

### B.9.2.5 e {#rb-turns.rate}

`turns.rate`

> The rate of turn must remain constant. Any change would be not more than a one (1) point deduction for each change.

### B.9.22.3 b {#rb-rolls.unlinked_pause}

`rolls.unlinked_pause`

> They must have a brief but perceptible pause between them, and they are to be flown in the same direction of rotation.

### B.9.23.1 {#rb-rolls.rate}

`rolls.rate`

> The penalty for varying the rate of roll is one (1) point per variation. Any stoppage in the aileron roll that could result in its being considered a hesitation roll, would hard zero (HZ) the figure.

### B.9.23.2 {#rb-rolls.stop}

`rolls.stop`

> The wings must stop precisely after the desired degree of rotation and not go past the stop point and then return. This is referred to as "bumping the point". A deduction of 0.5 point to one (1) point is awarded depending on the severity of the "bump"

### B.9.24.2 {#rb-rolls.hesitation_rate}

`rolls.hesitation_rate`

> The rate of the roll and the rhythm of the hesitations must be constant throughout with the aircraft projecting the pre-stated plane and direction of flight.

### B.9.24.3 {#rb-rolls.hesitation_pause}

`rolls.hesitation_pause`

> The pauses will be of identical duration. Each pause of a hesitation roll must be clearly recognizable in every case … If a pause is not recognizable to a judge, the figure is marked a Hard Zero (HZ).

### B.9.25.2 {#rb-snap_rolls.break}

`snap_rolls.break`

> The judge must see two things to determine that a flick roll has been correctly initiated: a) the aircraft must display a rapid and clearly visible change of pitch attitude to put the wing close to the stall, and b) autorotation must be initiated by use of the rudder. … However, if the required pitch change and/or actual autorotation are not clearly seen, the mark must be downgraded by four (4) points.

### B.9.25.3 {#rb-snap_rolls.definition}

`snap_rolls.definition`

> When, or shortly after, the fuselage pitches the glider must be seen to yaw, initiating a stall of one wing and the rapid onset of autorotation.

### B.9.25.3 {#rb-snap_rolls.pre_roll}

`snap_rolls.pre_roll`

> If the judge observes any movement about the roll axis before the autorotation starts, the figure must be downgraded one (1) point per five (5) degrees of roll.

### B.9.25.4 {#rb-general.autorotation}

`general.autorotation`

> Throughout the flick, the roll must be driven primarily by the rudder and autorotation must be seen to continue.

### B.9.25.4 {#rb-snap_rolls.exit}

`snap_rolls.exit`

> autorotation must stop as quickly as it started, after the desired extent of roll, followed immediately by the adoption of the attitude that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. Downgrades for minor errors in the extent of rotation or the following flight path or attitude are penalised at the normal rate of 1 point per 5 degrees.

### B.9.25.5 {#rb-snap_rolls.autorotation}

`snap_rolls.autorotation`

> in this case, a deduction of one (1) point for each five (5) degrees of rotation remaining when the autorotation ceases must be made. If autorotation ends with more than 45 degrees of rotation remaining, even if the roll is completed with aileron, the flick roll is awarded a numerical zero (0.0).

### B.9.26.1 {#rb-snap_rolls.negative}

`snap_rolls.negative`

> For negative flick rolls, all criteria stated for positive flick rolls apply … except that the aircraft is in a negative rather than positive angle-of-attack during autorotation.

### B.9.27.2 {#rb-spins.entry}

`spins.entry`

> All spins start from horizontal flight. In order to spin, the aircraft must be completely stalled on a clearly visible horizontal line near its minimum airspeed. In a correct spin entry, the nose of the glider drops and autorotation starts simultaneously around the longitudinal and vertical axes.

### B.9.27.4 {#rb-spins.stop}

`spins.stop`

> After completion of the prescribed number of turns, the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the pre-stated heading, then a 90 degree down, wings-level attitude must be seen.

### B.9.27.5 {#rb-spins.continue}

`spins.continue`

> Be alert for early stopping of the stalled autorotation followed by "aileroning" to the pre-stated heading. In this case, a deduction of one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of "aileroning" must be applied.

### B.9.27.6 {#rb-spins.attitude}

`spins.attitude`

> No account is to be taken of the pitch attitude of the aircraft during autorotation, as some aircraft spin in a nearly vertical attitude while others spin quite flat in conventional spins. Speed of rotation is also not a judging criterion.

### B.9.27.6 {#rb-spins.no_stall}

`spins.no_stall`

> If the aircraft never stalls, it is apparent that it cannot spin, and a downgrade by four (4) points must be given.

### B.9.27.7 {#rb-spins.definition}

`spins.definition`

> In all spins the marking criteria are: a) A clean breaking stall in horizontal flight. b) Fully stalled autorotation. c) Stopping on pre-stated heading. d) 90 degrees down, wings-level attitude after stopping on heading.

### B.9.27.7 d {#rb-spins.downline}

`spins.downline`

> 90 degrees down, wings-level attitude after stopping on heading.

### B.9.3.1 {#rb-turns.rolling}

`turns.rolling`

> The term “evenly integrated” means that from start to finish the figure should display a constant rate of turn combined with a constant rate of roll.

### B.9.3.6 c, B.9.3.6 d {#rb-turns.rolling_stop}

`turns.rolling_stop`

> Each stoppage of the rate of turn is a deduction of two (2) points. … Each stoppage of the rate of roll is a deduction of two (2) points.

### B.9.3.6 d {#rb-turns.rolling_rate}

`turns.rolling_rate`

> Each variation in the rate of roll is no more than a one (1) point deduction. Each stoppage of the rate of roll is a deduction of two (2) points.

### B.9.3.6 e {#rb-turns.rolling_reversal}

`turns.rolling_reversal`

> At a roll direction reversal there must be only a short pause, with the wings level. A longer pause is no more than a one (1) point deduction. Errors in the roll angle from wings level are deducted using one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.

### B.9.5.1 {#rb-stall_turns.definition}

`stall_turns.definition`

> In its most basic form, the figure begins when the aircraft leaves horizontal flight and flies a quarter loop to establish a vertical climb. At the top of the vertical line, the aircraft pivots and establishes a vertical descent, with the figure ending as the aircraft is returned to horizontal flight.

### B.9.5.2 e {#rb-lines.vertical_wings}

`lines.vertical_wings`

> During the vertical climb or vertical descent, the wings must remain parallel to the horizon. There will be a one (1) point deduction per five (5) degrees, when the line connecting both wing tips deviates from horizontal.

### B.9.5.2 f {#rb-stall_turns.pivot}

`stall_turns.pivot`

> To avoid a deduction, it must pivot around a point which should not be farther away from its centre of gravity than its wingtip. When the radius of the rotation is greater, the downgrade is one (1) point per half wingspan.

### B.9.5.2 h {#rb-stall_turns.pivot_motion}

`stall_turns.pivot_motion`

> There must be no rotation around the longitudinal or lateral axes. If there is movement around any axis other than the yaw axis, often referred to as "torquing" … there is a deduction of one (1) point for each five (5) degrees off axis.

### B.9.6.1 {#rb-tailslides.slide}

`tailslides.slide`

> At the point when the aircraft stops, it must slide backwards a visible amount (the key here is "a visible amount"). If a tailslide does not move backwards the reduction is -4,0 p.

### B.9.6.1, B.9.5.2 b, B.9.6.4 {#rb-tailslides.lean}

`tailslides.lean`

> All the criteria of the Stall Turn apply to this figure except, of course, for the manoeuvre at the top of the vertical climb. … Any deviation from vertical, either up or down, will result in a deduction of one (1) point per five (5) degrees from the zero-lift axis. … Wings should stay level with the horizon throughout and not drop during the slide or the fall through.

### B.9.6.2, B.9.6.3 {#rb-tailslides.recovery}

`tailslides.recovery`

> Following the slide backwards, the aircraft must then tip over and fall through to a diving position. The tipping over must be around the lateral axis only. Any movement around another axis is downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees. … Often the nose will swing back or "pendulum" past the vertical after falling through. The figure is not to be downgraded for this, nor downgraded if it does not happen.

### B.9.6.7 {#rb-tailslides.definition}

`tailslides.definition`

> In summary, the aircraft should make a smooth and steady transition up to vertical flight, the wings should stay level in relation to the horizon, and the aircraft should come to a complete stop in this attitude.
